title: Environmental and Green Chemistry
description: The chemistry of the atmosphere, water and pollution, and of making chemistry cleaner.

entries.name: The greenhouse effect and climate
entries.tagline: How gases in the air trap heat, and what is changing.

sections.text: Sunlight warms the surface of the Earth, which gives off the heat as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb some of that infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back to the surface. Without this natural effect the average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.
A gas absorbs infrared if its vibrations change the dipole of the molecule. CO₂, CH₄, N₂O and water vapor do. N₂ and O₂, the bulk of the air, do not.

facts: From burning fossil fuels, cement and deforestation. About 280 ppm before industry and over 420 ppm now. Stays in the air for centuries.
From livestock, rice fields, landfill and natural gas leaks. About 28 times as strong as CO₂ per molecule over a century, but it lasts about a decade.
From fertilized soil and industry. About 270 times as strong as CO₂ over a century.

sections.text: About a quarter of the CO₂ released by humans dissolves in the oceans. The surface ocean has become about 30% more acidic (pH down by about 0.1), which makes it harder for shellfish and corals to build shells of calcium carbonate.

quiz.q: Why do CO₂ and CH₄ act as greenhouse gases but N₂ and O₂ do not?
quiz.a: Their vibrations change the dipole, so they absorb infrared

entries.name: The ozone layer
entries.tagline: A thin shield of ozone that blocks harmful ultraviolet light, and how it was damaged.

sections.text: Ozone (O₃) in the stratosphere, 15–35 km up, absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. It is made and destroyed all the time in the Chapman cycle:

points: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once used in refrigerators and aerosols, are stable enough to reach the stratosphere. There, ultraviolet light breaks off chlorine atoms.
A chlorine atom destroys ozone in a catalytic cycle: Cl· + O₃ → ClO· + O₂, then ClO· + O → Cl· + O₂. The chlorine is regenerated, so one atom can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules.
In Antarctic spring, ice crystals in polar stratospheric clouds speed up the chemistry, which makes the ozone hole.

sections.text: The Montreal Protocol (1987) banned CFCs and has been one of the most successful environmental treaties. The ozone layer is slowly recovering and is expected to return to 1980 levels around the middle of this century.
Ozone high up protects us. Ozone at ground level is a harmful pollutant made from sunlight, nitrogen oxides and vapors from fuels and solvents.

quiz.q: Which chemicals were mainly responsible for the ozone hole?

entries.name: Acid rain and air pollution
entries.tagline: How burning fuel makes the rain and the air more acidic.

sections.text: Clean rain is slightly acidic, about pH 5.6, because it dissolves carbon dioxide. Acid rain is more acidic than that, mainly because of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Coal and oil contain sulfur. Hot engines and furnaces make nitrogen oxides by combining nitrogen and oxygen from the air.

points: Acidifies lakes and soils, harming fish and forests.
Attacks limestone and marble: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.
Corrodes metals.
Flue gas desulfurization: power station exhaust is passed through limestone slurry, which captures SO₂ as calcium sulfate.
Low-sulfur fuels.
Catalytic converters on cars use platinum, palladium and rhodium to turn harmful exhaust into harmless gases, for example 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂.

sections.text: In photochemical smog, sunlight breaks NO₂ into NO and O. The O atom forms ozone with O₂, which with unburnt fuel vapors makes the irritating brown haze seen over many cities.

quiz.q: What is the pH of normal, unpolluted rain?

entries.name: Water treatment and water quality
entries.tagline: How raw water is made safe to drink.

points: Screening removes large debris.
Coagulation: aluminium sulfate (alum) is added. It makes sticky aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃, which gathers the tiny suspended particles into clumps (flocs).
Sedimentation: the flocs sink and are removed.
Filtration through sand and gravel takes out the rest.
Disinfection kills the germs, with chlorine, ultraviolet light or ozone. Chlorine leaves a residue that keeps protecting the water in the pipes.
pH is adjusted, and in some places fluoride is added.

sections.text: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. It forms scale (CaCO₃) when heated and stops soap from lathering. It is softened by ion exchange, which swaps Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ for Na⁺, or by adding lime and soda ash to precipitate them.

points: Dissolved oxygen: fish need several mg/L. Pollution that consumes oxygen can suffocate them.
Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the oxygen that microbes use to break down the organic matter in a sample over five days. A high BOD means heavy organic pollution.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding alum in water treatment?
quiz.a: To clump tiny particles together so they can be removed

entries.name: Green chemistry
entries.tagline: Designing chemical processes to make less waste and use safer materials.

sections.text: Green chemistry aims to prevent pollution at the source, by designing products and processes that need fewer hazardous substances. Paul Anastas and John Warner set out 12 principles in 1998.

points: Prevent waste rather than clean it up.
Maximize atom economy.
Use safer solvents, and little or none.
Use less energy, at room temperature and pressure if possible.
Use renewable raw materials.
Use catalysts rather than large amounts of reagents.
Design products that break down after use.

equations: atom economy = (molar mass of the desired product ÷ total molar mass of all reactants) × 100%
sections.text: It shows how much of the starting material ends up in the product. Addition reactions, such as hydrogenation, are 100%. The esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate (88.11) from 60.05 + 46.07 = 106.12, so it is 83.0%, because water is lost.

The mass of waste per mass of product. Oil refining is below 0.1 and bulk chemicals are about 1 to 5, while fine chemicals and drugs can be 25 to over 100, which is why cleaner routes matter most there.

quiz.q: What is the atom economy of an addition reaction in which all the reactant atoms end up in the product?

entries.name: The carbon and nitrogen cycles
entries.tagline: How the key elements of life move between air, water, soil and living things.

points: Plants take CO₂ from the air in photosynthesis, and respiration and decay return it.
The oceans absorb and release CO₂ at the surface.
Fossil fuels are carbon stored for millions of years, and burning them moves it back into the air far faster than natural processes remove it.
Nitrogen fixation turns N₂ from the air into ammonia. It is done by bacteria in soil and root nodules, by lightning, and industrially by the Haber–Bosch process.
Nitrification: bacteria oxidize ammonia to nitrite and then to nitrate (NO₃⁻), which plants can take up.
Plants make proteins from nitrogen, and animals get it by eating plants.
Denitrification: other bacteria turn nitrate back into N₂, which returns to the air.

sections.text: Fertilizer from the Haber–Bosch process has roughly doubled the amount of fixed nitrogen entering the land. Runoff into water causes eutrophication, in which algae grow explosively, die, and use up the oxygen.

quiz.a: Turning N₂ from the air into ammonia
